lead: A photonic crystal is a dielectric whose refractive index repeats with a period comparable to the wavelength of light, in one, two or three dimensions. Waves reflected from the many repeated boundaries add in phase for a band of wavelengths, so light in that band cannot travel through the structure: that band is the photonic band gap. Breaking the pattern on purpose makes a defect that traps or guides light inside the gap. These ideas give near-perfect mirrors, tiny cavities, sharp bends on chips and fibers that guide light in a hollow core.

sections.h3: A one-dimensional crystal: the Bragg stack

blocks.text: The simplest photonic crystal is a stack of alternating layers: a high-index layer nH of thickness dH, then a low-index layer nL of thickness dL, repeated. The period a = dH + dL is one full pair of layers. At every interface a little light is reflected. When the reflections from successive periods return in phase, they add up and the stack reflects strongly. This is Bragg reflection, and at normal incidence it is centred on

λB = 2 n̄ a, n̄ = (nHdH + nLdL)/a
λB is the first-order centre wavelength of the reflection band (in vacuum); n̄ is the average index of one period, weighted by layer thickness; a is the period.

The strongest design is the quarter-wave stack, where each layer is a quarter wavelength thick in its own material: nHdH = nLdL = λB/4. Inside the band no wave can propagate through the periodic medium; the field decays from layer to layer, so a long enough stack reflects almost all of the light. Outside the band the stack passes most of the light, with small ripples.

The band is a range, not a line. For a quarter-wave stack its width in frequency is Δf/f₀ = (4/π) sin⁻¹[(nH − nL)/(nH + nL)], so a larger index contrast gives a wider gap. The peak reflectance rises with the number of pairs N. A stack with enough contrast can reflect a band for all angles of incidence and both polarizations: an omnidirectional reflector.

sections.h3: Two and three dimensions, and defects

blocks.text: A two-dimensional photonic crystal repeats in a plane, for example a triangular lattice of air holes etched through a thin silicon slab. A three-dimensional crystal repeats in all three directions, as in a woodpile of crossed rods or an opal of packed spheres; only a 3D crystal can have a complete gap that blocks every direction. In a 2D slab, light is held vertically by total internal reflection and in the plane by the gap.

A defect breaks the period and creates an allowed state inside the gap. Leave out one row of holes and the missing row becomes a line-defect waveguide: light at a gap wavelength cannot leak into the crystal on either side, so it follows the line, even round sharp corners. Leave out one or a few holes and you get a point-defect microcavity that stores light for many cycles in a volume about a wavelength across.

Fabrication methods follow the dimension: lithography and etching for 2D slabs; layer-by-layer stacking, self-assembly of spheres, and holographic lithography with interfering laser beams for 3D. Each trades precision against cost and area.

sections.h3: Photonic crystal fiber and practical limits

blocks.text: A photonic crystal fiber (PCF) has a regular array of air holes running along its length. In an index-guiding PCF the core is solid glass, the holey cladding has a lower average index, and a modified form of total internal reflection guides the light; the hole size and spacing set the mode area and dispersion, and some designs stay single-mode at every wavelength. In a band-gap PCF the periodic cladding forms a gap, so light can be guided in a hollow core of lower index than the glass, which no total-internal-reflection fiber can do. Hollow-core fibers carry high power, have very low nonlinearity and lower latency, because light travels mostly in air.

A photonic crystal is not loss-free by itself. Rough hole walls and errors in the period scatter light, the gap must sit on the source wavelength, and coupling to an ordinary fiber adds loss. For a 1550 nm gap with n̄ = 1.5 the period must be 1550/(2 × 1.5) = 517 nm, so the structure must be made to a few nanometres. The same Bragg rule designs thin-film filters, fiber Bragg gratings and laser mirrors.

examples.question: A quarter-wave mirror for 1550 nm is made of silicon nitride (n<sub>H</sub> = 2.0) and silica (n<sub>L</sub> = 1.45). Find (a) the two layer thicknesses and the period, (b) the average index and the Bragg wavelength, as a check, (c) the width of the stop band, (d) the peak reflectance of 8 pairs between air and a silica substrate, which a transfer-matrix calculation gives as 98.4 %, and the fraction transmitted.
steps: The band edges sit at f₀(1 ± 0.102), that is at λ = 1550/1.102 = 1407 nm and 1550/0.898 = 1726 nm: a stop band about 320 nm wide.
(d) R = 98.4 % at 1550 nm, so 1.6 % is transmitted. Fewer pairs reflect less: the same calculation gives 81 % for 4 pairs and 99.6 % for 10.
Check: using the plain mean (2.0 + 1.45)/2 = 1.725 instead of the thickness-weighted n̄ would predict 2 × 1.725 × 461.0 = 1590 nm, 40 nm off.
examples.answer: d<sub>H</sub> = 193.8 nm, d<sub>L</sub> = 267.2 nm, a = 461.0 nm, n̄ = 1.681 and λ<sub>B</sub> = 1550 nm; the stop band runs from about 1407 to 1726 nm, and 8 pairs reflect 98.4 % at its centre.

traps: The period a is one full pair of layers, not one layer.
n̄ in λ<sub>B</sub> = 2n̄a is weighted by thickness. The plain mean of n<sub>H</sub> and n<sub>L</sub> is correct only when both layers have equal thickness.
The gap is a band of wavelengths, not one wavelength; λ<sub>B</sub> is its centre.
Do not confuse the photonic band gap (a range of light wavelengths that cannot propagate) with a semiconductor's electronic band gap (an energy range with no electron states).
A band-gap fiber can guide in a hollow, lower-index core; an index-guiding PCF still needs the core index above the cladding's average.

quiz.a: A range of wavelengths (or frequencies) for which a periodic dielectric structure has no propagating mode, so light in that range is reflected or decays in the structure.

quiz.q: Why is the period taken as one full pair of layers in λ<sub>B</sub> = 2n̄a?
quiz.a: The structure repeats only after one high and one low layer, and the in-phase condition compares reflections from one period to the next; using a single layer would halve the predicted wavelength.

quiz.q: A stack has period 420 nm and average index 1.45. Find its first-order Bragg wavelength.
A stack must reflect at 1550 nm with n̄ = 1.5. Find the period.
Explain how removing one row of holes in a 2D photonic crystal makes a waveguide.
quiz.a: The missing row is a line defect that supports a mode at a wavelength inside the gap. Light in that mode cannot enter the perfect crystal on either side, because the crystal has no state there, so it is confined to the line and follows it, even round sharp bends.
A multilayer stack with enough index contrast that it reflects a band of wavelengths for all angles of incidence and both polarizations.

quiz.q: Using the worked example, why does raising the contrast from silica/nitride to silica/titania (n<sub>H</sub> about 2.3) widen the band?
quiz.a: The fractional width (4/π) sin⁻¹[(n<sub>H</sub> − n<sub>L</sub>)/(n<sub>H</sub> + n<sub>L</sub>)] grows with contrast: 0.85/3.75 = 0.227 gives Δf/f₀ = 0.291, against 0.204 for nitride. Each interface also reflects more, so fewer pairs reach the same reflectance.

beyond: Not for the exam. Photonic-crystal cavities on silicon give tiny lasers, filters and modulators, and hollow-core fibers are being deployed where low latency matters. Topological photonic crystals guide light along edges that tolerate defects. Search next for photonic crystal fiber, line-defect waveguide, nested antiresonant hollow-core fiber and the transfer-matrix method.
